notes.meaning: Festus was the new Roman governor of Judea. He lived in Caesarea, but after only three days he went up to Jerusalem. That city was still the center of Jewish worship and leadership, so he went to learn about the people he now ruled.

Two years had passed, but Paul's enemies had not let go. They moved fast, hoping a new governor would want to please them. They asked for a "favor": bring Paul to Jerusalem. Their real plan was to ambush and kill him on the road. Matthew Henry notes how strange it is to ask a judge for a favor against a prisoner when he has not been proven guilty.

Festus said no. Paul was safely held in Caesarea, and Festus was going back there soon. Any leaders who could prove a charge could come and make it there. We are not told why he refused, but the commentators see God quietly at work. A new ruler's choice kept Paul alive, just as God had promised Paul he would testify in Rome (Acts 23:11).
After a short stay of eight or ten days, Festus went back to Caesarea. He wasted no time. The very next day he took his seat as judge, which made it a formal court, and had Paul brought in.

The Jewish leaders crowded around Paul and piled up serious charges. It looks like they hoped to scare the judge and the prisoner. But a Roman court needed proof, and they had none. Calvin notes that Christ's servants are often falsely accused, even when they have done good.

Paul's short answer shows the three charges: breaking the Jewish law, defiling the temple, and acting against Caesar, the Roman emperor. He denied all three. Preaching Christ, who fulfills the law, was no crime against the law. The charge against Caesar was the most dangerous one, because it would have meant treason.

Festus wanted to win the Jewish leaders' goodwill. So he asked Paul to agree to a trial in Jerusalem. If he had wanted simple justice, he would have let Paul go. Because Paul was a Roman citizen, Festus seems to have needed his consent. Wesley sees God guiding even this, so that Paul would have reason to appeal to Rome.

Festus judged in the emperor's name, so his court was really "Caesar's judgment seat." As a Roman citizen, Paul had the right to be tried there and not handed to his enemies. He boldly reminded Festus that he knew Paul was innocent. Matthew Henry says it is right for innocent people to defend their good name.

Paul was not trying to dodge justice. If he deserved death, he would accept it. But no one could "give him away" to his enemies as a favor. Every Roman citizen had the right to appeal to the emperor, so Paul used it. Calvin and Barnes say Christians may rightly use the protection of the law, and this step also led Paul to Rome, where he had long wanted to go.

Festus talked it over with his own advisers, not the Jewish council. Then he granted the appeal. Some hear a touch of annoyance in his words, as if to say "see if you do better there." Barnes thinks he was also glad to be free of a hard case.

King Agrippa II was the great-grandson of Herod the Great and son of the Herod who killed James (Acts 12). He ruled lands to the north, including part of Galilee. Bernice was his sister, and many suspected the two had a shameful relationship. They came to honor the new governor, since Agrippa's power depended on Rome's goodwill.

During their long visit, Festus told the king about Paul. Agrippa was a Jew and knew Jewish matters better than Festus did, so Festus may have wanted his advice. He described Paul as a prisoner Felix had left behind.

The leaders wanted Paul condemned without a hearing. Festus told them Romans did not hand a man over to death as a favor. First the accused must meet his accusers face to face and defend himself. Matthew Henry and Wesley say Christians should follow this same rule and never judge others without hearing their side.
Festus held the hearing right away. With so much anger aimed at Paul, he expected to hear of some terrible crime. To his surprise, nothing like that was charged against him.

Festus called it a quarrel about their religion and about "a certain Jesus" who had died, but whom Paul said was alive. He spoke of it lightly. Yet without meaning to, he named the very heart of Paul's message: Jesus rose from the dead. Matthew Henry says all the business of the Roman Empire was small next to this question.

Festus said he didn't know how to look into such religious questions, so he had offered Paul a trial in Jerusalem. Luke already told us his real motive was pleasing the Jews (v. 9). When Paul appealed to the emperor (here called "Augustus," meaning Nero), Festus kept him under guard until he could be sent.

Agrippa politely asked to hear Paul himself. He had surely heard a lot about Jesus and the Christians, and he was curious. The Geneva Notes see God's promise coming true here: Paul would carry Christ's name before kings (Acts 9:15).

Agrippa and Bernice arrived with great show, along with army officers and the city's leading men. It was not a trial but a grand gathering. Matthew Henry says the chained prisoner, with his faith, courage, and holiness, had more true glory than all their fine clothes. Calvin notes this gave Paul a famous audience to preach Christ to.

Festus told the gathering that the Jews, in Jerusalem and in Caesarea, had shouted that Paul should die. But he admitted he had found nothing in Paul worthy of death. Matthew Henry says this public word from the judge honored Paul. Still, Festus did not set him free.

Festus had nothing solid to write to the emperor, whom he called "my lord." It made no sense to send a prisoner without stating the charges. So he hoped Agrippa, who knew Jewish ways, could help him. Robertson and Calvin note that by saying this, Festus showed he should have freed Paul.
